use_case: Pre-procedural neuraxial landmark identification for spinal/epidural access
clinician_control: full - clinician performs all imaging and needle placement
regulatory_status: FDA 510(k) K171594 cleared 2017-10-20, product code IYO (System Imaging Pulsed Echo Ultrasonic), Class II, 21 CFR 892.1560
evidence: vendor clinical literature and independent trials; not audited in this project
strongest_feature: Only cleared handheld device purpose-built for neuraxial landmark identification; genuine market validation of the clinical need
limitation: Handheld - reproducibility still depends on operator; no robotic acquisition; no force control; no needle tracking
opportunity_for_us: Robot-held acquisition removes the operator-variability term that a handheld device cannot address; our contribution is acquisition standardisation, not landmark detection per se

regulatory_status: FDA 510(k) K243937 cleared 2025-05-23, product code IYO, Class II
strongest_feature: Active product line iteration - the incumbent is investing
opportunity_for_us: Confirms the segment is commercially live; differentiation must be acquisition + workflow rather than a better landmark classifier

regulatory_status: FDA 510(k) K253452 cleared 2026-07-24, product code IYO, Class II
strongest_feature: Most recent clearance in the family
opportunity_for_us: Shows regulatory cadence of roughly annual iteration

regulatory_status: FDA 510(k) K254021 cleared 2026-04-09, product code IYO, Class II
limitation: Scope of XV not verified in this project
opportunity_for_us: Watch for scope expansion beyond neuraxial

regulatory_status: FDA 510(k) K250469 cleared 2025-06-13 and K261014 cleared 2026-07-24, product code ITX (Transducer Ultrasonic Diagnostic), Class II, 21 CFR 892.1570
strongest_feature: Demonstrates that a passive, disposable needle guide is a viable regulatory and commercial object in this segment
limitation: Passive alignment only - no active repositioning, no feedback
opportunity_for_us: Direct precedent for the consumable-guide element of Architecture B/D and for a consumable revenue line

product_or_system: Robot-assisted lumbar ultrasound acquisition platform (FAROS project)
use_case: Robot-acquired lumbar spine ultrasound with CT ground truth
probe_force_control: yes - 5 N target contact force, 20 N maximum, 4 mm/s maximum velocity
clinician_control: robot performs scanning only; no needle involvement
evidence: 63 healthy volunteers, 223 handheld + 375 robotic scans, 6091 annotated frames from 9 subjects
strongest_feature: The only in-vivo human paired handheld/robotic lumbar ultrasound dataset with CT ground truth, released CC-BY
limitation: Healthy young volunteers only; prone position; 10 MHz linear probe; bone-surface labels only; no needle and no procedural targets
opportunity_for_us: Closest prior art to our acquisition concept. They solved robot-acquired lumbar imaging; nobody has connected it to a clinician-authored procedural target layer. That gap is our thesis.

use_case: Injury localisation and anatomical segmentation on exposed spinal cord
ai: yes (YOLOv8 / DeepLabv3 / SegFormer / U-Net / TransUNet / Swin-UNet / SAMed)
evidence: YOLOv8 mAP50-95 0.606 for injury localisation; DeepLabv3 mean Dice 0.587 on porcine; SAMed mean Dice 0.445 zero-shot on human
strongest_feature: Largest annotated spinal cord ultrasound dataset released publicly; rigorous two-stage clinical label review
limitation: Intraoperative after laminectomy; porcine; not neuraxial access anatomy; no licence declared on the release
opportunity_for_us: Provides an ultrasound-domain pretraining corpus and a realistic benchmark for cross-species/cross-domain generalisation methodology

use_case: CT-to-ultrasound registration validation for image-guided spinal surgery
ultrasound: yes (real US on ex-vivo phantoms only)
evidence: 21 landmark pairs per phantom with fiducial silver-standard registration
patients_or_phantoms: 3 human subjects (CT + simulated US only), 2 ex-vivo animal phantoms
strongest_feature: Openly licensed (CC-BY-4.0) registration benchmark with landmark ground truth
limitation: Human ultrasound is SIMULATED from CT - there is no real human US in the release; phantoms are ex-vivo exposed bone
opportunity_for_us: Useful only as a registration-algorithm testbed; documents how thin the real public spine-US pool is

evidence: ~100k ex-vivo human lower-limb ultrasound images with algorithmically generated, physics-refined bone labels
strongest_feature: Demonstrates automated CT-derived labelling at a scale manual annotation cannot reach - directly relevant to our annotation-cost problem
limitation: Lower limb not spine; ex-vivo; labels are algorithmic not expert; public availability NOT confirmed
opportunity_for_us: The automated-labelling methodology is the transferable idea: if CT-registered auto-labelling works for limbs, it is the obvious route to scaling lumbar labels beyond what clinicians can hand-draw

product_or_system: Automatic lumbar level identification and landmark detection in ultrasound
use_case: Automated identification of lumbar level and vertebral landmarks
ai: yes (classical phase-based features through to CNNs)
evidence: Representative works: automatic lumbar level identification (2008); automatic lumbar anatomy detection (2010); phase-based bone localisation (2009); spinous process + acoustic shadow segmentation (2016); filter-layer-guided CNN bone segmentation (2019)
patients_or_phantoms: human volunteers and patients across studies
strongest_feature: A 15+ year literature already solves much of the perception problem - level ID and landmark detection are not open research questions
limitation: Fragmented; mostly single-centre; rarely released data or code; almost never connected to acquisition hardware or to procedural outcome
opportunity_for_us: Confirms that another landmark detector is NOT a defensible contribution. The unsolved parts are acquisition standardisation, clinician-authored targets, uncertainty and outcome linkage.
